meta.title: Who really said "A man who has never gone to school may steal from a freight car; but if he has a university education, he may steal the whole railroad"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Roosevelt. The joke was already running in American newspapers in 1899 as an unsigned Chicago News filler paragraph; the oldest Roosevelt credit is from 1952.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A man who has never gone to school may steal from a freight car; but if he has a university education, he may steal the whole railroad'?
meta.ogDescription: No Roosevelt source exists. The joke ran unsigned in the Chicago News in 1899, and Mother Jones was using her own version of it in 1903 — in a speech aimed at Roosevelt.

answer.label: Not Theodore Roosevelt — an 1890s newspaper joke
answer.authorDates: Unattributed · documented in an unsigned newspaper paragraph of 1899
answer.sourceLine: There is no Roosevelt source. Wikiquote lists the line among his disputed quotations and traces the credit no further back than a 1952 book on public speaking — but the Library of Congress newspaper archive has it pinned on him seven years earlier than that, in a Veterans of Foreign Wars newsletter of 1 March 1945 ↗, twenty-six years after he died. The joke itself is older than any of the credits: a version was already running as unsigned newspaper filler in January 1899, and Mother Jones was using her own form of it in a 1903 speech — a speech addressed, as it happens, to President Roosevelt.

source.heading: What is actually documented

docMeta.dd: 1 March 1945 · Monthly News of the Department of Washington (Veterans of Foreign Wars) · Chronicling America ↗

source.excerpt: A ten-year-old lad in Indianapolis who was arrested for picking up coal along side of railroad tracks is now in jail. If the boy had known enough to steal the whole railroad he would be heralded as a Napoleon of finance.
trail: Wikiquote does not put this in Roosevelt’s sourced material. It sits in the Disputed section, and the earliest citation given for it is The Art of Communicating Ideas (1952) by William Joseph Grace, page 389 Wikiquote — Roosevelt, disputed ↗.

Wikiquote’s Rail transport page traces the sentiment to an unsigned item in the Chicago News, reported in the Locomotive Engineers Journal volume 33 (1899), page 69, and states plainly that “the origin of the sentiment is often erroneously attributed to Theodore Roosevelt” Wikiquote — Rail transport ↗.

We confirmed that 1899 paragraph independently rather than take it on trust, and it reads exactly as quoted above: The Pocahontas Times (Huntersville, West Virginia), 19 January 1899, page 1, in the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America archive, printed as filler and credited “—Chicago News.” (We are citing that page rather than linking it: the Library of Congress viewer refuses automated requests, so we could not confirm the link resolves for a reader.)

The best-known relative of the joke is Mother Jones’s: “I asked a man in prison once how he happened to be there and he said he had stolen a pair of shoes. I told him if he had stolen a railroad he would be a United States Senator.” It is in chapter 10 of her Autobiography, in a Coney Island speech from the 1903 March of the Mill Children Autobiography of Mother Jones, Project Gutenberg ↗ — a speech whose whole point was to demand that President Roosevelt act on child labour.
source.excerptNote: This is not the sentence at the top of this page. It is the oldest form of the joke we were able to locate and read for ourselves: an unsigned filler paragraph credited to the Chicago News, reprinted in The Pocahontas Times of Huntersville, West Virginia, on 19 January 1899, page 1, in the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America collection.
source.rightsNote: The wording on this page has no identified author, so no rights status can honestly be asserted for it. The two documented texts behind it are a different matter: the 1899 Chicago News paragraph and Mother Jones’s Autobiography (1925) are both long out of copyright in the United States. Roosevelt’s own published writings are public domain too — but this sentence is not among them. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Theodore Roosevelt
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Roosevelt
author.bio: Theodore Roosevelt is one of the most quotable presidents and one of the most over-quoted. He wrote prolifically and spoke constantly, which makes a plausible-sounding aphorism hard to disprove by ear — and his reputation as a trust-buster makes anti-monopoly wisecracks stick to him in particular. Wikiquote’s page for him carries a long disputed section; this line is in it.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: A line about educated men stealing on a grander scale sounds like the trust-busting president, which is most of why it gets pinned on him. What is missing is any occasion on which he said it.

items.why: The line appears in Wikiquote’s Disputed section with a 1952 earliest citation Wikiquote ↗, and a full-text search of English Wikisource — whose author page for him lists more than 80 books, essays and addresses Wikisource — Theodore Roosevelt ↗ — returns no instance of the phrase anywhere in the library.

A boy jailed in Indianapolis for taking coal from beside the tracks, against the financier who takes the railroad and is called a Napoleon of finance. Same joke, different sentence, and printed while Roosevelt was still governor of New York Wikiquote — Rail transport ↗.
Her version swaps the freight car for a pair of shoes and the railroad for a Senate seat, and she aimed it at Roosevelt rather than borrowing it from him Autobiography of Mother Jones ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment is real, old and American; the attribution is not. Nobody has produced a Roosevelt source, and the joke was in print before he was president Wikiquote — Rail transport ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to him
lead: Roosevelt’s trust-busting reputation rests substantially on a railroad case. His Justice Department sued the Northern Securities Company — one of the first antitrust cases filed against corporate interests rather than labour — won, and had the company dissolved, so that its three railroads operated independently again Northern Securities Company — Wikipedia ↗. A wisecrack about the man who steals the whole railroad and walks free reads as something he might have growled at a reporter.

The irony is that the joke belonged to the people pushing him. Mother Jones was firing her version of it at Roosevelt from a stage at Coney Island in 1903, with mill children in animal cages beside her, trying to get him to act on child labour. A generation later the line came back with his name on it.
detailsBody: No Roosevelt source has ever been produced for this sentence, in his writings, speeches or letters.
Wikiquote’s earliest datable attribution to him is a 1952 book on public speaking — thirty-three years after his death.
The joke is documented in an unsigned Chicago News paragraph reprinted on 19 January 1899, when Roosevelt had been governor of New York for less than three weeks.
Mother Jones used her own form of it in 1903, in a speech demanding that President Roosevelt act on child labour.
A full-text search of the whole of English Wikisource, whose author page for Roosevelt lists more than 80 of his works, returns no instance of the phrase.
context.pull: The joke was aimed at Roosevelt long before it was credited to him.
